questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain the Fallacies most clearly committed in the following arguments:

(i) Top ranking officials argue that governmental decisions are the best because they have been carefully scrutinized by government officials.

(ii) Many Cameroonians in the diasporas say they sponsor Charity Organisations because other Cameroonian are doing so.

(iii) After ringing the bell for assembly, the physically challenged student was asked to run up along other students to the assembly ground.

(3 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Begging the question (petitio principii), or circular reasoning (3 marks).** The conclusion is "governmental decisions are the best". The only reason given is that the decisions "have been carefully scrutinized by government officials", that is, by the same body that took them. The reason already assumes that the government's own judgement is reliable, which is exactly what has to be proved. The argument runs in a circle: the decisions are good because officials approve them, and officials are to be trusted because they are officials. No independent check (an auditor, a court, the public) is offered. The speakers are also judging their own cause, which weakens the argument further, but the main fault is that the conclusion is smuggled into the premise.

**(ii) Bandwagon (argumentum ad populum, appeal to the majority) (3 marks).** The only reason given for sponsoring charity organisations is that "other Cameroonians are doing so". The fact that many people do something is not a reason to think that it is right, useful or good. The argument appeals to popularity and to the wish to belong, instead of giving the real reasons that would justify the sponsorship (the needs of the beneficiaries, the results of the organisations). Charity may well be good, but this reasoning does not show it.

**(iii) Fallacy of accident (applying a general rule to an exceptional case) (3 marks).** The general rule is that students run to the assembly ground when the bell rings. The person who gives the order applies it without exception to a physically challenged student, for whom a special circumstance (the disability) makes the rule unsuitable. The "accidental" circumstance is ignored, and a rule that holds in general is applied to a case it was never meant to cover, which makes the order unreasonable and unfair.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Put the following arguments into Valid standard form:

(i) Only mothers are farmers; Farmers are not business persons; Mothers are never business persons.

(ii) Not all prophets are preachers; Each preacher is an intellectual; Prophets are not generally intellectuals.

(2 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A categorical syllogism in standard form has three propositions, each of type A, E, I or O, with the **major premise** (the one containing the major term $P$) first, then the **minor premise** (containing the minor term $S$), then the conclusion ($S - P$). The last proposition of each argument is the conclusion.

**(i) (3 marks).**
- "Only mothers are farmers" is an exclusive proposition: it means *all farmers are mothers* (A).
- "Farmers are not business persons" means *no farmers are business persons* (E).
- "Mothers are never business persons" means *no mothers are business persons* (E).

Terms: $S$ = mothers (minor), $P$ = business persons (major), $M$ = farmers (middle).

> Major premise: No farmers are business persons. (E)
>
> Minor premise: All farmers are mothers. (A)
>
> Conclusion: Therefore, no mothers are business persons. (E)

The middle term is the subject of both premises: **Third Figure, mood EAE**. Test of validity: "mothers" is distributed in the conclusion (subject of an E) but is undistributed in the minor premise (predicate of an A), so the form commits the **illicit minor**. It is invalid (a set-model check in Python confirms it): there may be mothers who are not farmers and who are business persons. The only conclusion that follows from these two premises is the particular "Some mothers are not business persons" (EAO, Felapton), valid only if there are farmers.

**(ii) (3 marks).**
- "Not all prophets are preachers" means *some prophets are not preachers* (O).
- "Each preacher is an intellectual" means *all preachers are intellectuals* (A).
- "Prophets are not generally intellectuals" means *some prophets are not intellectuals* (O).

Terms: $S$ = prophets, $P$ = intellectuals, $M$ = preachers.

> Major premise: All preachers are intellectuals. (A)
>
> Minor premise: Some prophets are not preachers. (O)
>
> Conclusion: Therefore, some prophets are not intellectuals. (O)

The middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise: **First Figure, mood AOO**. Test: "intellectuals" is distributed in the conclusion (predicate of an O) but not in the major premise (predicate of an A): **illicit major**; moreover, in the First Figure the minor premise must be affirmative and here it is negative. The argument is invalid (confirmed by a set-model check in Python): there can be prophets who are not preachers but who are intellectuals.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Use the truth table to prove the validity or invalidity of the following arguments:

(i) $M$; $N$; $\therefore M \cdot N$

(ii) $R \vee (S \supset T)$; $S \cdot \sim R$; $\therefore \sim R$

(2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
An argument is **valid** if there is no row of its truth table in which all the premises are true and the conclusion is false. The rows in which all premises are true are in bold.

**(i) $M$, $N$ / $\therefore M \cdot N$ (2 marks).**

| $M$ | $N$ | premise 1: $M$ | premise 2: $N$ | conclusion: $M \cdot N$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **T** | **T** | **T** | **T** | **T** |
| T | F | T | F | F |
| F | T | F | T | F |
| F | F | F | F | F |

The only row in which both premises are true is the first, and the conclusion $M \cdot N$ is true there. **The argument is valid** (this is the rule of conjunction).

**(ii) $R \vee (S \supset T)$, $S \cdot \sim R$ / $\therefore \sim R$ (2 marks).**

| $R$ | $S$ | $T$ | $S \supset T$ | premise 1: $R \vee (S \supset T)$ | $\sim R$ | premise 2: $S \cdot \sim R$ | conclusion: $\sim R$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T | F | F | F |
| T | T | F | F | T | F | F | F |
| T | F | T | T | T | F | F | F |
| T | F | F | T | T | F | F | F |
| **F** | **T** | **T** | **T** | **T** | **T** | **T** | **T** |
| F | T | F | F | F | T | T | T |
| F | F | T | T | T | T | F | T |
| F | F | F | T | T | T | F | T |

The only row in which both premises are true is $R$ = F, $S$ = T, $T$ = T; there the conclusion $\sim R$ is true. **The argument is valid.** (It is even trivially valid, since the conclusion $\sim R$ is one of the two conjuncts of the second premise.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) Symbolized the following arguments by using the appropriate variables p and q:

(i) Either Adamu is the teacher or Musa is a nurse. Adamu is a teacher. Therefore, Musa is a nurse.

(ii) If the rain falls, then the harvest will be abundant. The harvest will not be abundant. Therefore, the rain does not fall.

(iii) Politicians are either sailors or painters. Politicians are sailors. Therefore, Politicians are not painters.

(3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Each simple statement is replaced by a variable; the connectives are written with the usual symbols.

**(i) (2 marks).** $p$ = Adamu is the teacher; $q$ = Musa is a nurse.

$$
\begin{array}{l}
p \vee q \\
p \\
\therefore q
\end{array}
$$

This is the form "affirming a disjunct". It is **invalid**: with $p$ = T and $q$ = F both premises are true and the conclusion $q$ is false. Affirming one disjunct does not permit the conclusion that the other disjunct is true.

**(ii) (2 marks).** $p$ = the rain falls; $q$ = the harvest will be abundant.

$$
\begin{array}{l}
p \supset q \\
\sim q \\
\therefore \sim p
\end{array}
$$

This is **modus tollens**, a valid form.

**(iii) (2 marks).** $p$ = politicians are sailors; $q$ = politicians are painters.

$$
\begin{array}{l}
p \vee q \\
p \\
\therefore \sim q
\end{array}
$$

This form is valid only if "either...or" is read as **exclusive** (exactly one of the two); with the inclusive "or" it is invalid (the premises are true and the conclusion false when $p$ and $q$ are both true).
